verdict.root_cause: The live symptom is latency, not failure. checkoutservice completes every PlaceOrder stage successfully but per-order duration grew from ~30ms at 06:56 to several hundred ms by 07:27-07:28, while its error ratio rose ~8x (0.17% -> 1.4%, peak ~10%) in spiky bursts with change points at 07:05:15 and 07:11:15 — the shape of a caller intermittently breaching deadlines on a slow callee, not of a caller broken in itself. cartservice shows no errors, no restart, no Redis trouble and steady multi-RPC-per-second service through 07:28, which is exactly how a pod looks when delay is imposed on its network path rather than inside its process. The cartservice change stream is a scheduled fault-injection harness (platform-automation) whose arms include a traffic-shaping container imposing 300ms of eth0 delay on the cart network namespace — a magnitude matching the observed per-order growth. I blame slow cart-path calls, with checkoutservice, frontend and loadgenerator alerting only because they wait on it. The key tension: the record shows the delay container removed at 05:52 and the last cart change reverted at 06:09, so no recorded injection was in force at 07:05 onset — hence low confidence.
verdict.reasoning: [tr_076ff865351b] shows checkoutservice healthy in kind but degraded in time: all PlaceOrder stages succeed, throughput continues, no error lines, yet per-order duration grows tenfold across the window. [tr_00e7b9ffcbe2] dates the real onset to 07:05-07:11, twenty minutes before the alert, with intermittent bursts rather than sustained failure — deadline breaches on a waited-upon call. [tr_43eb80e8a7ae] rules out cartservice crash, Redis loss and wedge, so cartservice is not failing internally; it is slow or delayed on the wire. [tr_4409a3aae327] shows this exact service is the standing target of a repeating 300ms eth0 delay injection, matching the observed magnitude — while also recording that arm as removed at 05:52, which is the main strike against this verdict. [tr_8a6753c7f6a9] returned no samples in either window, so cartservice's own error rate and latency could not adjudicate.
open_questions: No cartservice-side latency or request-rate measurement exists ([tr_8a6753c7f6a9] empty in both windows), so the 300ms delay is inferred from checkout timestamp spacing, never measured at the source.
Both log results are truncated to oldest 8 / newest 32 lines, so 07:05-07:27 — the interval containing actual onset — is uncovered on both services.

No result attributes checkoutservice errors to cartservice specifically; the metric carries no downstream-peer dimension, and 4 unmeasured edges were crossed, so another callee (paymentservice, emailservice, productcatalog) could be the slow dependency.

alternatives.root_cause: A different downstream of checkoutservice (payment, email, catalog or the queue) became slow, and cartservice is innocent — triage simply started there.
alternatives.why_not: Same mechanism, less specific target: no evidence names an alternate slow callee, whereas cartservice has a documented 300ms delay-injection harness aimed at it. Kept because [tr_00e7b9ffcbe2] cannot attribute errors to any peer.

alternatives.root_cause: The fault-injection harness left a cart configuration override (REDIS_ADDR pointing at redis-cart:6380) partially in force, making cart operations slow or erratic.
alternatives.why_not: [tr_43eb80e8a7ae] shows cartservice connected to redis-cart:6379 with a passing self-test and no Redis errors through 07:28, and [tr_4409a3aae327] records the override reverted at 06:09; a wrong address would produce cart-side errors, which are absent.

proposal.expected_effect: No action is proposed, so no change in system behaviour is expected. The observable state should continue as recorded: checkoutservice error ratio elevated (~1.4% mean, ~10% peak) in spiky bursts, per-order PlaceOrder duration in the hundreds of milliseconds, cartservice logging several successful RPCs per second with no errors. The next useful step is measurement, not mutation: a per-peer latency/error query from checkoutservice (grouped by downstream peer) and an untruncated log pull across 07:05-07:27 on both services would either name the slow callee or exonerate cartservice.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if evidence appears that a fault-injection arm was actually in force at 07:05-07:28 — e.g. a change-history entry showing a traffic-shaping container or REDIS_ADDR override applied after 06:09 and not yet reverted, or a cartservice-side latency series showing ~300ms added on the cart path. It is also wrong if a per-peer breakdown attributes checkoutservice's error bursts specifically to cart RPCs. Either would meet revert_config's preconditions and make a targeted revert on cartservice the right call. Conversely, if the delay is real but imposed by a sidecar this system cannot address, the effect of any permitted action would be unobservable and abstention remains correct.
proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is that the latency persists and continues to convert into checkout errors for callers, so user-visible order latency and the ~1.4% error ratio stay elevated for as long as it takes to gather the missing measurements. The risk of the alternative — proposing revert_config on cartservice anyway — is worse and concrete: the change record shows the last cartservice config (REDIS_ADDR) was already reverted at 06:09, so 'restoring the previous configuration' would re-apply REDIS_ADDR=redis-cart:6380, pointing a currently-healthy cartservice (clean Redis connect at 05:33, no Redis errors through 07:28) at a non-default port and turning a latency incident into a hard cart outage. revert_config's preconditions are not met: no configuration change is named inside the incident window, only reverts before it.
proposal.blast_radius: Nothing changes, so nobody sees a change from this proposal. The population already affected and still affected is: checkoutservice (elevated errors, slow PlaceOrder), and its upstreams frontend and loadgenerator, which alert only because they wait. cartservice itself shows no degradation. Had revert_config been proposed against cartservice, the blast radius would have been cartservice plus every caller of it — checkoutservice and frontend — including a connection reset during container recreate, plus redis-cart seeing traffic move to the alternate address.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Four services alerted within seconds along the cart/checkout/frontend path, which is a coordinated user-facing failure rather than an isolated warning. No open incident covers it, and the shared timing suggests a downstream dependency degrading upstream callers.
